questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Allied plans for liberated Europe

options.misconception: misreads the dispute as a question of reparations money
options.text: An argument over what the liberated states should pay back afterward

questions.explanation: Each side assumed the next government would take the shape its occupier gave it, so free elections implied a rival program of appointed loyalists, and neither plan could be conceded without handing the other a continent. questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Ending a confrontation without war
questions.learningObjective: design a step that lowers tension under time pressure
questions.stem: A confrontation has reached the point where each side's next move would be read as the step before war, and a third party asks both to lower the tension. Which approach is most likely to end it?

options.misconception: makes the public cost fall on the one who moves
options.text: Announce a deadline, then punish the first side to soften

options.misconception: mistakes disclosure for de-escalation
options.text: Reveal each side's worst fears in order to increase pressure

options.misconception: assumes an outsider will take the dispute
options.text: Let the third party settle every disputed question itself

questions.explanation: The danger lies in a move that cannot be taken back once the other side has read it as the step before war, so removing that reading by making the disputed move observable changes what either side believes it is about to face. The tempting answers reward whoever moves first, add pressure to an already unstable situation, or assume an outsider can settle a dispute it does not own.
questions.hint: Which part of the danger is an inference, not a fact?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading the arithmetic of the 1970s
questions.learningObjective: interpret planning figures as a budget of commitments
questions.stem: A planning table for the middle 1970s shows industrial output rising about four percent a year, fuel import costs rising tenfold after a supply cut, and military outlays fixed at a share of state spending that could not be cut without losing the alliance's protection. What does that table let an official conclude?

options.text: That the current growth could not pay for the current costs

options.misconception: assumes defense cuts are politically available
options.text: That recovery followed automatically once military spending fell

options.misconception: makes one price rise explain all the strain
options.text: That the import bill alone explains every later shortage

options.misconception: answers a cost question with a value judgment
options.text: That the alliance was worth more than the growth it consumed

questions.explanation: Growth of four percent could not absorb a tenfold rise in the one item a state had to buy abroad while a defense bill fixed in share grew alongside it, so the table measures a gap that no single price or policy choice would close, and that gap is what made reform look desperate. The tempting answers each remove one of the three lines the others depend on.
questions.hint: Can four percent growth outrun a tenfold price rise?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading a worker's strike and its reversal
questions.learningObjective: analyze why an agreement was withdrawn
questions.stem: Read the record: workers at a shipyard in an eastern European state stop work, the government agrees to higher wages and an independent union, and within eighteen months it cannot pay the wages because the price of everything it sells abroad has fallen, so it cancels the agreement and outlaws the union. What does that sequence show?

options.misconception: invents an electoral motive the record lacks
options.text: That the leaders chose the strike to avoid a general election

options.misconception: makes a lost income a planned conspiracy
options.text: That the government had planned the reversal from the start

options.misconception: claims a prior refusal the record contradicts
options.text: That the workers had rejected the settlement before it began
That concessions had to be reversed when the income vanished

questions.explanation: The concessions were priced in the currency of foreign sales, and when that price fell the same agreement that had been affordable became a bill the government could not pay, so the retreat was arithmetic before it was political. The tempting answers require a planned scheme, a political motive, or a prior rejection, and the record shows a sequence of events instead.
questions.hint: What were the promised wages actually paid in?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reforming a centrally planned economy
questions.learningObjective: design a reform that the managing elite will carry out
questions.stem: A state has run its economy by central plan for decades, and the officials who manage every plant refuse to support a reform that lets managers set their own prices. Which change is most likely to make the reform hold?

options.misconception: denies the managers any stake in the result
options.text: Call the reform temporary, so no manager is asked to choose
Let a plant keep the earnings its own decisions produce

options.misconception: tightens the control the reform must relax
options.text: Place every plant directly under a ministry in the capital

options.misconception: keeps the plan's targets as the governing rule
options.text: Give each ministry its own output targets for the decade

questions.explanation: A reform survives only if the people who can stop it gain from carrying it out, and letting a plant keep what its own results earn turns the manager from the roadblock into the official who benefits, whereas a decree leaves every manager with a reason to wait. The tempting answers keep the new rules in the hands of the old system, so the resistance stays exactly where it was.
questions.hint: Who has the power to make a reform fail quietly?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a border crossing ended a rivalry in 1989
questions.learningObjective: analyze how a system lost control of its own border
questions.stem: In the autumn of 1989 crowds began crossing a wall that had divided a city for nearly three decades, guards stopped manning the checkpoints, the crossing was opened in the middle of the night without announcement, and within a year the two states that had built their systems around that border were gone. What made the difference?

options.misconception: treats masonry as if it were an intention
options.text: The barrier had been designed to hold crowds permanently

options.misconception: invents a treaty that never restricted the border
options.text: An old agreement had always forbidden closing the crossing
Controls had more to lose from enforcing than from failing

options.misconception: assumes a military agreement nobody negotiated
options.text: Rival armies had already agreed to meet at the crossing

questions.explanation: A border holds while the machinery around it is staffed and believed in, and once the state across it had stopped punishing people for crossing, the guards doing the work were no longer protected by anyone, so the safe post became the open one. The tempting answers treat masonry or an agreement as the cause, when the cause was how many people found the closure no longer worth enforcing.
questions.hint: Who was left exposed once the other side stopped arresting people?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The agreement to limit missile defenses
questions.learningObjective: identify the reasoning behind limiting missile defenses
questions.stem: In 1972 the two largest powers agreed neither would build missile defenses against the other, and they said offense was cheaper than defense and that defenses made the attacking side feel safer first. What did that reasoning aim at?

options.misconception: confuses a limit on defense with an end to weapons
options.text: A promise that neither side would build any new weapons

options.misconception: reads a limit on defense as a limit on industry
options.text: An agreement to close both countries' heavy industries

options.misconception: claims a testing halt the treaties did not contain
options.text: A shared halt on testing every kind of new weapon
To keep both sides able to absorb a strike and answer it

questions.explanation: A defense that can be overcome still provokes an attack before it is finished, and a state that believed its missiles were safe would strike first, so limiting defenses left both sides dependent on their own power to retaliate, which is what each feared most. The tempting answers read the limit as disarmament, deindustrialization, or a testing halt, and the reasoning concerned the ability to absorb and answer.
questions.hint: What would a country with a working defense feel tempted to do?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Designing a commitment that can be ended
questions.learningObjective: design a commitment that does not renew itself
questions.stem: A government has backed a distant ally with money and advisers for years, each annual renewal now costs more, and the ally's position grows harder to hold every season. Which commitment design most reduces the cost of saying no later?

options.misconception: makes the term depend on the ally's behavior
options.text: Promise support for as long as the ally remains loyal
Fund outcomes on a fixed term that expires unless renewed

options.misconception: keeps the ratchet that created the cost
options.text: Raise the yearly sum so the ally cannot say no either

options.misconception: hides the cost without shortening the term
options.text: Transfer the commitment to another government to administer

questions.explanation: A commitment that renews by choice can be ended, while one that renews by precedent is defended by everyone who draws from it, so writing an expiry into the original terms turns saying no into a scheduled decision rather than a betrayal, which is the only way the yearly cost stops growing. The tempting answers tie the term to loyalty, keep the ratchet that produced the problem, or move the paperwork while the promise stays open-ended.
questions.hint: What makes an open-ended promise safe to end?
